A personal cybersecurity portfolio, lab notebook, and practical knowledge base.

I work across cyber-fraud monitoring, security operations, and technical investigation. Privacy Skill Vault is where I document the concepts I study, the environments I build, the tools I test, and the investigation methods I refine.

The goal is straightforward: make technical work understandable, reproducible, and honest about what has actually been tested.

docs.title: How information is labelled
docs.text:
Accuracy matters more than presentation. Content is identified by its evidence level:

  • Professional experience — generalised and sanitised descriptions; no employer, customer, or internal system details.
  • Lab-tested — performed in a controlled environment, with relevant setup and limitations recorded.
  • Simulated scenario — constructed for learning; not represented as a real incident.
  • Research note — based on documentation or external references and not yet independently validated.

docs.text:

docs.title: Detection Engineering — Operational Pack
docs.text:
Reference pack — validate against your own telemetry before enabling

This pack contains two Windows detections with Sigma source, Elastic KQL and Splunk SPL equivalents, synthetic test cases, and a repeatable release procedure. It is designed to be adapted—not imported blindly—into a real SIEM.

docs.title: Scope and source assumptions
docs.text:
Component Assumption used in this pack Must be confirmed in the target environment Endpoint telemetry Windows Security log and Sysmon Operational log Windows build, audit policy, Sysmon version/configuration, event forwarding Sigma Sigma Rules Specification 2.1.0 Installed Sigma CLI and backend/pipeline versions Elastic ECS-compatible fields; Elastic Security Elastic Stack, integration version, data stream, mappings, rule type Splunk Raw Sysmon XML/event fields Splunk version, index, sourcetype, field extractions, CIM mapping ATT&CK Technique IDs listed on each analytic ATT&CK release used by your organisation

Important: the Elastic and Splunk queries below are authored equivalents for the stated field assumptions. They are not generated output from a verified converter run and are not asserted to work unchanged against every deployment. The Sigma YAML files are authored against the published Sigma structure; they still require parsing, backend conversion, and data-level testing in the target stack.

docs.title: Included detections
docs.text:
1. PowerShell encoded-command execution — Sysmon Event ID 1 / process creation.
  2. Addition to the local Administrators group — Windows Security Event ID 4732.

docs.title: Sysmon process creation
docs.text: Microsoft documents Sysmon Event ID 1 as Process Create, with process image, command line, parent process, hashes and Process GUID available according to configuration and event version. Process creation logging is a prerequisite for the PowerShell analytic. Sysmon Event ID 3 network connections are disabled by default; do not assume they are collected.

docs.title: Windows Security group management
docs.text: Windows Security Event ID 4732 records a member added to a security-enabled local group. The event is generated on domain controllers, member servers and workstations. Configure and verify the applicable Advanced Audit Policy and event forwarding; absence of an event is not proof that no group change occurred.

docs.title: Validation lifecycle
docs.text:
For each rule, use the following release gates:

  1. Confirm the source event is generated locally on a controlled test endpoint.
  2. Confirm the same event arrives in the SIEM and inspect its raw payload.
  3. Confirm each required field is populated and mapped as expected.
  4. Parse the Sigma file with the current Sigma toolchain and convert it with the intended backend and processing pipeline.
  5. Compare converted output with the native query; review any semantic differences.
  6. Run positive, negative and benign-administration test cases.
  7. Review duplicates, alert context, search latency, event volume and query cost.
  8. Obtain peer review and change approval before enabling in production.
  9. Monitor the analytic and document tuning, owner, rollback and next review date.

docs.title: Sigma CLI reference workflow
docs.text:
The Sigma project documents installation of sigma-cli, backend plugins, and conversion with a selected backend and processing pipeline. For a controlled workstation:

python -m pip install 'sigma-cli==3.1.0'
sigma plugin install splunk
sigma plugin install sysmon
sigma convert -t splunk -p sysmon docs/detection-engineering/rules/windows-powershell-encoded-command.yml
sigma convert -t splunk -p splunk_windows docs/detection-engineering/rules/windows-local-admin-membership.yml

This repository's CI pins Sigma CLI 3.1.0 because the currently published Sysmon pipeline is not compatible with pySigma 2.x; do not force-install an incompatible plugin. Recheck the Sigma CLI releases, Sysmon pipeline releases, and plugin compatibility before upgrading. CI converts the Sysmon process-creation rule to Splunk SPL using the Sysmon pipeline and the Windows Security Event 4732 rule using the Splunk Windows pipeline. These are parser/backend conversion checks only; they do not test the generated queries against a live Splunk instance or genuine telemetry. A successful conversion proves that the selected toolchain accepted the rule for that backend; it does not prove that the query matches your telemetry or detects malicious activity.

docs.title: Operational ownership
docs.text:
Every production rule should have: - A named service and technical owner. - A documented data-source owner and telemetry-health check. - A severity/priority mapping approved by the organisation. - An analyst runbook and escalation route. - A versioned query, test set and change history. - A suppression/exception owner and expiry/review date. - A rollback procedure and disablement authority.

Do not use Sigma level as a substitute for your incident severity matrix. Sigma metadata and organisational incident priority are different concepts.

docs.title: Detection 002 — Addition to local Administrators group
docs.text: Review privileged change; validate local group scope

docs.title: Analytic intent
docs.text:
Identify Windows Security Event ID 4732 where the target group SID is the built-in local Administrators group SID S-1-5-32-544. This indicates a membership addition to that security-enabled local group. It does not establish whether the change was authorised.

  • Rule ID: PSV-WIN-002
  • Sigma ID: 2b3e1e76-7e3b-4a9d-9d81-001000000002
  • Data source: Windows Security log, Event ID 4732
  • ATT&CK mapping: T1098.007 — Additional Local or Domain Groups
  • Initial Sigma level: high
  • Status: test

docs.title: Required event fields
docs.text:
Field Meaning EventID 4732 — member added to a security-enabled local group TargetSid SID of the target group; expected built-in Administrators SID for this analytic TargetUserName / TargetDomainName Resolved target group name/domain, if available MemberName / MemberSid Account added to the group SubjectUserName / SubjectDomainName Actor recorded as performing the change SubjectLogonId Logon session identifier for correlation on the same host

Group display names may be localised or renamed. The well-known SID is a more stable selector for the built-in local Administrators group, but confirm that the event field is correctly parsed and that your environment's group semantics match this analytic.

docs.title: Sigma rule
docs.text:
Source file: windows-local-admin-membership.yml

title: Member Added to Built-in Local Administrators Group
id: 2b3e1e76-7e3b-4a9d-9d81-001000000002
status: test
description: Detects a member added to the built-in local Administrators group using Windows Security Event 4732.
author: Privacy Skill Vault
date: 2026/10/31
logsource:
    product: windows
    service: security
detection:
    selection:
        EventID: 4732
        TargetSid: 'S-1-5-32-544'
    condition: selection

    - SubjectUserName
    - SubjectDomainName
    - SubjectLogonId
    - MemberName
    - MemberSid
    - TargetUserName
    - TargetSid

    - Approved endpoint provisioning
    - Privileged access management workflows
    - Software deployment or support activity

tags:
    - attack.persistence
    - attack.privilege_escalation
    - attack.t1098.007

docs.title: Elastic Security — KQL starting query
docs.text:
Assumptions: Windows Security events are ingested and the raw Windows event data is available in winlog.event_data.

event.code : "4732"
and winlog.event_data.TargetSid : "S-1-5-32-544"

Check the actual field mapping in Discover before deploying. Some integrations expose additional normalised fields; retain the original raw event fields for auditability.

docs.title: Splunk — raw Windows Security SPL starting query
docs.text:
Replace the index and source value with values verified from your deployment. The CI conversion using the Sigma Splunk Windows pipeline emits the source constraint shown here; your ingestion configuration may use a different source/sourcetype mapping.

index=YOUR_INDEX source="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4732 TargetSid="S-1-5-32-544"
| table _time host SubjectUserName SubjectDomainName SubjectLogonId MemberName MemberSid TargetUserName TargetSid

docs.title: Test matrix
docs.text: Test Event Expected Positive 4732, TargetSid S-1-5-32-544 Match Negative 4732, TargetSid S-1-5-32-545 (Users) No match Negative 4735 group changed, no 4732 member-add event No match Benign positive Approved IT provisioning adds a technician Match; verify ticket, requester, approver and device scope Coverage gap Security audit event not generated/forwarded No detection; record telemetry gap

docs.title: Analyst triage
docs.text:
1. Confirm the host and original event XML; verify TargetSid, MemberSid, actor, time and logon ID.
  2. Identify the added principal by SID and directory source; determine whether it is a user, computer or service account.
  3. Confirm whether the target is the local Administrators group on an endpoint or a different group with a similar name.
  4. Correlate the actor's logon session, process creation, remote administration activity, change ticket and privileged access records.
  5. Determine whether the member was newly created, recently enabled, or used for subsequent interactive/network logons.
  6. Search for follow-on privileged activity and lateral movement from the affected host.
  7. Record the authorisation decision and evidence. Containment or removal requires the organisation's approved authority and change process.

docs.title: Tuning
docs.text: Do not blanket-exclude IT administrators or provisioning accounts. Tune by approved workflow identity, source host, target group, actor, ticket evidence and expected timing. Every exception needs an owner and periodic review.

docs.title: Detection 001 — PowerShell encoded-command execution
docs.text: Triage signal, not malware verdict

docs.title: Analytic intent
docs.text:
Identify PowerShell process-creation events whose command line includes the commonly used `-EncodedCommand` / `-enc` parameter. Encoded commands can be used by administrators and software deployment tools as well as adversaries. This analytic flags the execution pattern for review; it does not decode the payload, establish malicious intent, or prove compromise.

  • Rule ID: PSV-WIN-001
  • Sigma ID: `2b3e1e76-7e3b-4a9d-9d81-001000000001`
  • Data source: Sysmon Operational, Event ID 1
  • Sigma logsource: Windows / process_creation
  • ATT&CK mapping: T1059.001 — PowerShell (behavioural mapping, not attribution)
  • Initial Sigma level: medium
  • Owner: Detection Engineering
  • Status: test

docs.title: Required telemetry
docs.text:
Field Purpose Expected source Event ID Process creation event Sysmon Event ID 1 Image Executable path Sysmon `Image` CommandLine Process command line Sysmon `CommandLine` ParentImage Parent executable context Sysmon `ParentImage` ProcessGuid / ParentProcessGuid Stronger process correlation than PID alone Sysmon GUID fields User Execution identity Sysmon user field, where populated

Do not silently substitute Windows Security Event ID 4688 for Sysmon Event ID 1. Windows process-creation auditing can be used as a separate source, but command-line collection requires the relevant policy and has different field semantics.

docs.title: Sigma rule
docs.text:
Source file: windows-powershell-encoded-command.yml

```yaml title: PowerShell Encoded Command Execution id: 2b3e1e76-7e3b-4a9d-9d81-001000000001 status: test description: Detects PowerShell process creation with an encoded-command argument. Review context; this is not a malware verdict. author: Privacy Skill Vault date: 2026/10/31 logsource: product: windows category: process_creation detection: selection_image: Image|endswith: - '\powershell.exe' - '\pwsh.exe' selection_encoded: CommandLine|contains: - '-EncodedCommand ' - '-encodedcommand ' - '-enc ' - '-ENC ' condition: selection_image and selection_encoded fields: - Image - CommandLine - ParentImage - User - ProcessGuid - ParentProcessGuid falsepositives: - Approved software deployment or endpoint management scripts - Administrative automation using encoded PowerShell - Security products or installers that launch encoded PowerShell level: medium tags: - attack.execution - attack.t1059.001 ```

The Sigma file is provided as source. CI validates it against the Sigma 2.1.0 JSON schema and converts it using Sigma CLI 3.1.0 with the Splunk backend and Sysmon processing pipeline. This does not test the generated query against a live Splunk instance or real telemetry. Before operational use, test it against raw events from the target SIEM and confirm the installed backend/pipeline compatibility. Schema validation does not prove detection semantics, backend compatibility, or production effectiveness.

The explicit command-line patterns are intentionally conservative and may miss unusual quoting, parameter abbreviations, or obfuscation. Expand only after testing the resulting noise and coverage.

docs.title: Elastic Security — KQL starting query
docs.text:
Assumptions: the Windows/Sysmon integration maps process creation into ECS fields and the selected data view contains the events.

```kql event.code : "1" and process.name : ("powershell.exe" or "pwsh.exe") and process.command_line : (-EncodedCommand or -encodedcommand or -enc) ```

If the actual integration maps the executable or command line differently, inspect the raw document and correct the mapping. Do not assume every deployment populates `process.name` from Sysmon `Image`.

docs.title: Splunk — raw Sysmon SPL starting query
docs.text:
Replace `YOUR_INDEX` and the sourcetype with the actual values in your deployment. Confirm field extractions from a raw event first.

```spl index=YOUR_INDEX sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" EventID=1 | where match(Image, "(?i)\\\\(powershell|pwsh)\\.exe$") AND match(CommandLine, "(?i)(^|\\s)-(enc|encodedcommand)(\\s|$)") | table _time host User Image CommandLine ParentImage ProcessGuid ParentProcessGuid ```

This SPL uses raw Sysmon field names. If your collector uses a different sourcetype or normalises to CIM, adapt the query to the observed schema. Do not copy an index or sourcetype name from this example into production.

docs.title: Test matrix
docs.text: Test Input Expected Positive PowerShell image and `-EncodedCommand` argument Match Positive PowerShell image and `-enc` argument Match Negative PowerShell with `-File` only No match Negative `cmd.exe` with text containing `-EncodedCommand` No match Benign positive Approved management script using encoded PowerShell Match, then close as expected activity with owner/change evidence Telemetry gap Sysmon Event ID 1 not collected No detection; record as coverage gap, not a true negative

docs.title: Analyst triage
docs.text:
1. Retrieve the full event and adjacent process events for the host and time window.
  2. Correlate by Sysmon Process GUID and Parent Process GUID where available; use PID only with host and time because PIDs are reused.
  3. Identify the parent process, user, integrity context, executable path, signer, hash and command-line context.
  4. Decode the command only in an approved, isolated analysis workflow. Treat decoded content as untrusted.
  5. Correlate file creation, DNS, network, PowerShell Operational logs, EDR telemetry and change-management records.
  6. Check whether the script, parent process, account and execution time match an approved administrative task.
  7. Record evidence, alternative explanations, confidence and data gaps. Escalate using the organisation's incident process.

docs.title: Tuning and release
docs.text:
• Do not suppress all encoded PowerShell or all activity from a management agent.
  • Build narrow exceptions from verified signer, path, parent, host role, account and approved change context; set an owner and expiry.
  • Review positive and negative tests after every exception change.
  • Measure event delay, alert volume, benign-positive rate, investigation context and missed-test cases.
  • Obtain peer review and change approval before enabling.

docs.text: Every report must distinguish observed evidence from interpretation. Published material is classified as sanitised professional experience, lab investigation, simulated scenario, or research note. No customer records, internal banking details, production IP addresses, or employer-confidential information belong here.

docs.title: Detailed walkthrough
docs.text: • Suspicious PowerShell from a Scheduled Task — a synthetic evidence-led investigation with competing hypotheses, correlation steps, and an analyst checklist.

docs.title: Worked example: suspicious PowerShell launched by a scheduled task
docs.text:
SIMULATED TRAINING SCENARIO

Hostnames, timestamps, commands, and indicators in this example are synthetic. It does not describe a real customer, employer, or production incident.

docs.title: Initial alert
docs.text: A monitoring rule flags encoded PowerShell launched by a scheduled-task process outside an expected maintenance window.

docs.title: Investigation questions
docs.text:
1. What process created PowerShell, and what was its full command line?
  2. Which account and integrity level were involved?
  3. Is the scheduled task known, approved, and correctly owned?
  4. Do script-block, process, DNS, proxy, and firewall records corroborate the activity?
  5. Is there evidence of payload retrieval, persistence, lateral movement, or impact?

docs.title: Evidence to correlate
docs.text:
• Process creation telemetry, including parent process and command line
  • PowerShell operational events where logging is enabled
  • Scheduled-task registration and execution history
  • DNS and network connection records
  • File creation, hash, signature, and reputation context
  • Change records and owner confirmation

docs.title: Example reasoning
docs.text: An encoded command is a triage signal, not proof of malware. A scheduled task can be legitimate administration or unauthorised persistence. Validate the task definition, executable path, script contents, account, creation time, change history, and network destinations before assigning a verdict.

docs.title: Possible outcomes
docs.text:
• Expected administration: document the owner and maintenance purpose; tune narrowly with evidence.
  • Policy violation: remediate the configuration even if malicious intent is not established.
  • Likely compromise: follow incident-response procedures, preserve evidence, and consider containment under organisational policy.
  • Insufficient evidence: state what telemetry is missing and what additional collection is required.

Avoid treating one event or one indicator as a complete story. Record confidence, alternative explanations, data gaps, and the basis for every conclusion.

docs.title: Account Takeover (ATO) Investigation Playbook
docs.text: Operational reference — follow approved bank procedures

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Provide a repeatable evidence-led investigation for suspected digital-channel account takeover, including disputed transactions. This playbook is a checklist and decision aid; it does not authorise account restrictions, transaction blocks, customer contact, or regulatory notifications.

docs.title: 1. Establish the case and preserve evidence
docs.text:
Record the case ID, alert/reference IDs, customer/account reference in the authorised case platform, detection source, time first observed, investigator, case owner, current status, and approved priority.

Preserve original records before enrichment or transformation. Record source system, native event ID, event timestamp and time zone, collection time, record/request/trace/session identifiers, collector, export method, integrity hash where supported, and access restrictions.

Do not paste customer identifiers, authentication secrets, full card data, OTPs, session tokens, or internal production logs into this public template or an unapproved service.

docs.title: 2. Build a single timeline
docs.text:
Normalise timestamps to UTC while retaining the original timestamp and offset. Use a timeline table:

UTC time Source Event / action Actor / account Device / session IP / channel Transaction Evidence reference [time] [IAM/app/fraud/core] [login/profile change/payment] [masked ID] [ID] [IP/channel] [ID] [record ID]

Do not correlate solely on a timestamp. Prefer server-issued identifiers and independently observed keys: authentication request ID, session ID, API request/trace ID, transaction ID, payment reference, 3DS transaction identifiers, device attestation reference, and account/customer key. Record the reliability and origin of each identifier.

docs.title: 3. Evidence collection matrix
docs.text: Domain Collect Questions / caveats Identity provider / IAM Login attempts, success/failure, MFA challenge/result, password reset, recovery, authenticator enrolment/removal, lockout, token/session issue and revocation Which component authenticated the user? Which factor was actually validated? Mobile/web application App version, device ID and fingerprint, device attestation result if implemented, session creation/refresh/revoke, API route, request/trace ID, server response Was the identifier generated client-side or server-side? Could it be copied or replayed? API gateway / WAF Request ID, trace ID, route, method, source IP, TLS/client metadata available, status, upstream target and latency Was the call received, rejected, retried, or routed elsewhere? Fraud platform Rule/model version, evaluated features, score, decision, reason codes, latency, override, bypass/disable event, operator and configuration history What exact data was evaluated at decision time? Were rules disabled or thresholds changed? Core banking / payment Transaction ID, posting/authorisation state, amount, currency, beneficiary, rail, timestamps, reversals/returns, channel and authorisation references Distinguish initiated, authorised, accepted, posted, settled, reversed and returned states. Device / endpoint EDR events, device registration, OS/app version, root/jailbreak/attestation signals, malware findings, integrity signals A matching device ID is not proof of the same physical device or legitimate user. Network / infrastructure IP, port, ASN/geo enrichment, DNS, proxy, VPN indicators, firewall, load balancer, NAT and TLS metadata IP and geolocation are contextual signals; consider carrier NAT, VPNs, proxies and shared egress. Customer / channel Contact history, verified callback result, dispute details, known travel/accessibility context where lawfully available Use independently verified contact routes and approved customer-contact scripts. 3-D Secure / card rails Protocol version, message identifiers, result/status, challenge flow, ECI and other fields supplied by the provider Interpret fields with the applicable EMVCo version and provider mapping. Authentication result is not a complete fraud verdict.

docs.title: 4. Correlation logic
docs.text:
Use the following sequence and record each join:

  1. Link the disputed transaction to the payment/core record using the authoritative transaction or payment reference.
  2. Link the transaction to the fraud decision using the decision reference, rule execution ID or trace ID.
  3. Link the fraud decision to the application/API request using a server-side request or trace ID.
  4. Link the API request to the authenticated session using the session reference; establish whether the mapping is direct or inferred.
  5. Link the session to the authentication event using the identity provider's authentication/request ID and user/account key.
  6. Link the session/device to network and endpoint evidence using multiple attributes and timestamps, not a client-controlled device ID alone.
  7. Independently compare the resulting chain with customer dispute evidence and known-good historical behaviour.

A join that relies only on approximate time, IP, user-agent or a client-generated device ID must be labelled a weak correlation—not a confirmed link.

docs.title: 5. When the session is missing from logs
docs.text:
Do not conclude that a session did not exist merely because it is absent from one log source. Investigate the logging path:

  • Was the session created by a different component, region, API version, gateway, or authentication provider?
  • Is the expected event generated at all, or only after a successful downstream step?
  • Was the log sampled, filtered, dropped, delayed, overwritten, or outside retention?
  • Are clocks out of sync or time zones misinterpreted?
  • Did an asynchronous queue, retry, cache, or service-to-service call break trace propagation?
  • Are request IDs and trace IDs regenerated at a proxy or gateway?
  • Did the request fail before application logging, or did a downstream service accept a request without the expected upstream log?
  • Was there a logging configuration change, service restart, audit disablement, or pipeline incident?
  • Can the provider, API gateway, WAF, load balancer, mobile telemetry, or core system independently corroborate the request?

Document the exact sources searched, query/time range, retention status, and whether the source is expected to log that event. Use the conclusion “not present in the available source records” until the gap is explained.

docs.title: 6. Assess device-ID cloning or replay hypotheses
docs.text:
A cloned or reused device identifier is a hypothesis to test, not a conclusion based on duplicate values alone.

Compare: - Client device ID against server-side device registration and attestation references. - App instance ID, app version, OS build, device model and integrity signals. - Concurrent or near-concurrent sessions using the same identifier from incompatible network contexts. - Device ID history, reset/re-registration events and identifier lifecycle. - TLS/client metadata and API request patterns where lawfully collected. - Authentication factors, session tokens and token lifecycle; do not expose token values in the case report. - Differences between mobile telemetry, API gateway records and fraud-platform feature inputs.

Possible explanations include identifier cloning/replay, legitimate app reinstall or migration, SDK changes, shared devices, account sharing, data mapping defects, stale cache, or a provider integration issue. Seek independent evidence before choosing among them.

docs.title: 7. Assess transaction and customer impact
docs.text:
Record each disputed transaction separately. Distinguish attempted, declined, authorised, posted, settled, reversed, returned and recovered amounts. Record currency, fee/FX impact, beneficiary, rail, transaction status, dispute status, and any related transactions.

Determine whether the same session/account/device/beneficiary or fraud pattern affects other customers. Use approved internal link-analysis and case-management controls.

docs.title: 8. Decision and escalation
docs.text:
Escalate according to approved policy when there is credible evidence of ongoing unauthorised access, attempted/confirmed financial loss, compromised credentials or sessions, multiple affected customers, suspected control bypass, or a material logging/control failure.

For any protective action, record: - Decision-maker and authority - Evidence and risk basis - Exact scope (account/session/device/transaction) - Execution time, operator and system result - Customer/service impact - Review and reversal criteria

Do not infer a mandatory action or deadline from this playbook. Use the institution's current policy, payment scheme rules, contracts, and applicable regulatory obligations.

docs.title: 9. Case conclusion
docs.text:
State one of: confirmed unauthorised activity; likely unauthorised activity; suspicious but inconclusive; legitimate/authorised activity; control/process failure without confirmed fraud; or unable to determine. Define the institution's approved case outcomes if they differ.

Include observed facts, correlated facts, analysis, alternative hypotheses, confidence, losses/attempts, customer impact, control gaps, actions and approvals, evidence gaps, root cause (if supported), corrective actions, owners and target dates.

docs.title: Payment Fraud Investigation Playbook
docs.text: Operational reference — not payment-scheme advice

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Structure an investigation into suspected unauthorised card, account-to-account, bill-payment or other digital payment activity. Use the actual payment rail and provider documentation; do not assume every rail exposes the same lifecycle states, identifiers or reversal rights.

docs.title: 1. Preserve the transaction record
docs.text:
For each transaction, record the authorised case reference and the authoritative values available in the payment/core system:

  • Transaction/payment reference and any parent/related reference
  • Channel, product, payment rail and provider/acquirer
  • Initiation, authorisation, acceptance, posting, settlement, reversal/return timestamps
  • Amount, currency, fees and FX conversion (where applicable)
  • Debtor/payer account reference and beneficiary/payee reference (masked in reports)
  • Status, response/decline codes, reason codes and source system
  • Fraud decision reference, rule/model version, score, decision and override
  • Authentication method and result, including 3DS where applicable
  • Customer dispute/contact record and source of the statement

Do not collapse “authorised”, “posted”, “settled”, “reversed” and “refunded” into a single “successful” state. Confirm the meaning of each status with the system or payment provider.

docs.title: 2. Reconstruct the payment flow
docs.text:
Map the real message and service path for the specific rail. A generic card-not-present flow may involve customer channel, merchant, 3DS Server, Directory Server, Access Control Server, acquirer, issuer authorisation host and payment network. A SADAD or other account/bill-payment flow has a different path and must be mapped from the bank/provider's own interface and operational documentation.

For every hop, record request/response IDs, timestamps, system name, status and the original event reference. Confirm which system is authoritative for each state.

docs.title: 3. Card-not-present and 3-D Secure evidence
docs.text:
When 3DS is involved, capture only fields actually present in the issuer/acquirer/provider records and interpret them using the applicable EMVCo specification version and integration documentation.

Potentially relevant fields include: - Protocol version - threeDSServerTransID, dsTransID, and acsTransID where supplied - messageType and messageVersion - transStatus and transStatusReason, where present - challengeCompletionInd and challenge-flow evidence, where present - ECI and authentication value/reference as represented by the network/provider - Directory Server / ACS result, error and timeout information - Provider mapping of authentication, authorisation and liability-related outcomes

Protect authentication values and sensitive payment data. Store the minimum necessary evidence in the authorised case system; do not publish full values in PSV.

Do not assume: a generic “3DS passed” label means the legitimate account holder initiated the transaction; a frictionless flow means the customer actively approved it; or a liability-shift indicator determines the bank's fraud verdict. Confirm the actual protocol version, result fields, scheme rules and provider semantics.

docs.title: 4. Account-to-account, bill-payment and SADAD-style flows
docs.text:
For a non-card payment, identify the rail-specific source of truth and collect: - Payment initiation request and response references - Payer authentication and authorisation records - Beneficiary validation and any beneficiary creation/change event - Payment provider/SADAD reference and status history, where applicable - Core banking debit/credit posting and reconciliation records - Limit checks, fraud decision and rule/model evaluation - Cancellation, reversal, return, dispute or recovery state - Customer channel and session linkage

Do not apply EMV 3DS fields to a rail that does not use EMV 3DS. Do not assume a payment can be reversed or blocked after a particular state without checking the applicable rail and operating procedure.

docs.title: 5. Fraud-control evaluation
docs.text:
For every relevant decision, reconstruct what the control knew at decision time:

Question Evidence Which control evaluated the transaction? Rule ID, model/version, policy version What input features were available? Feature snapshot or decision audit record What was the output? Score, reason code, approve/decline/step-up/review result Was the control operating? Health/availability, timeout, fallback and bypass logs Was the decision changed? Override actor, reason, approval and timestamp Was the same pattern seen elsewhere? Related cases, accounts, devices, beneficiaries and transaction references Was the control calibrated? Test results, false-positive/false-negative review, change history

A missing fraud alert does not by itself prove a rule failed. First establish whether the event reached the engine, whether required features were present, whether the rule was enabled and in scope, and whether the decision was logged.

docs.title: 6. Cross-system correlation
docs.text:
Correlate payment reference → fraud decision reference → API request/trace ID → authenticated session → authentication event → device/network evidence. Use independent references wherever possible. Record the join key, source and confidence for every link.

If an application session is absent, use the dedicated ATO playbook to investigate logging and trace-propagation gaps. Do not fill missing records with assumed values.

docs.title: 7. Scope, loss and customer impact
docs.text:
• Identify related transactions and whether the pattern spans customers, channels, products, beneficiaries or institutions.
  • Separate attempted, declined, authorised, posted, settled, reversed, returned and recovered amounts.
  • Record gross and net loss using the institution's accounting definition; do not add amounts across statuses in a way that double-counts.
  • Confirm customer impact and contact status using approved processes.
  • Preserve evidence for dispute, scheme, provider, legal and regulatory processes as required.

docs.title: 8. Outcome and corrective action
docs.text:
The case conclusion should identify confirmed facts, inference, alternative explanations, confidence, loss status, customer impact, control performance, evidence gaps and unresolved questions.

Potential corrective-action categories include: - Authentication or account-recovery control - Device binding/attestation and session management - API authentication, authorisation and trace propagation - Fraud-rule/model feature quality, coverage and calibration - Transaction limits, beneficiary controls and step-up decisions - Logging, monitoring, evidence retention and case workflow - Third-party/provider integration and reconciliation

Assign each action an accountable owner, approval, risk rationale, due date, validation evidence and closure criteria. Do not use a generic remediation deadline or severity threshold unless approved by the institution.

docs.title: Investigation Walkthrough: Suspicious PowerShell from a Scheduled Task
docs.text:
Simulated training scenario

This case is synthetic. Host names, timestamps, users, event records, and command lines are invented for training. It is not a description of a real customer, employer, bank, or production incident.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
An endpoint alert reports PowerShell execution shortly after a scheduled task was created on a workstation. The command line contains encoded content. The analyst must determine whether this is expected administration, a policy violation, or evidence of compromise.

Initial alert is not a verdict. Encoded PowerShell, an unfamiliar task, or an unusual parent process can justify investigation, but none independently proves malicious activity.

docs.title: Investigation objectives
docs.text:
1. Establish what happened and when.
  2. Identify the account, process, task definition, and affected host.
  3. Correlate independent endpoint, identity, and network telemetry.
  4. Test benign and malicious explanations.
  5. State the conclusion, confidence, evidence gaps, and recommended next steps.

docs.title: Synthetic evidence set
docs.text:
Time (UTC) Source Synthetic observation 09:12:04 Endpoint alert Encoded PowerShell execution detected on WS-TRAIN-07 09:11:58 Process telemetry powershell.exe started; parent process and full command line available 09:10:31 Task audit A scheduled task registration was recorded; task XML and registering account require retrieval 09:12:10 DNS telemetry A query was recorded shortly after process start; destination context is not yet established 09:12:18 Network telemetry One outbound connection was observed; process attribution must be corroborated

These rows are intentionally incomplete. They provide investigation leads, not proof that the task, DNS query, and connection belong to one causal chain.

docs.title: Step 1 — Preserve and scope
docs.text:
• Record the alert ID, host identifier, event source, original timestamps, collection time, and analyst actions.
  • Preserve the original event records and task definition before making changes.
  • Confirm the host owner, business function, maintenance window, and whether an approved change exists.
  • Establish whether similar activity appears on other endpoints.
  • Record which telemetry sources are available and their retention windows.

Do not modify or delete the task before preserving the relevant evidence unless an authorised containment decision requires immediate action.

docs.title: Step 2 — Reconstruct process execution
docs.text:
Review the process event and collect, where available:

  • Image path, hash, signer, and file metadata
  • Full command line and parent command line
  • Parent and child process identifiers or process GUIDs
  • User, logon session, integrity level, and host
  • Process start and termination times

Validate the parent-child relationship using the raw event. Parent process names can vary by Windows version and execution path; do not assume one fixed Task Scheduler process chain.

For Sysmon, Event ID 1 is Process Create. Its presence depends on Sysmon installation and configuration. Correlate process identifiers and timestamps rather than relying only on process names.

docs.title: Step 3 — Inspect the scheduled task
docs.text:
Retrieve the task's:

  • Full task path and name
  • Registration and modification times
  • Author and security principal
  • Trigger and execution conditions
  • Action, executable path, arguments, and working directory
  • Run level and task history
  • Creation or modification source, where available

Compare the task definition with the organisation's approved software deployment, administration scripts, and change records. A task can be legitimate, misconfigured, or unauthorised; classify it only after checking ownership and intent.

docs.title: Step 4 — Correlate independent telemetry
docs.text:
Evidence source Questions to answer Important limitation Windows process telemetry Which process launched PowerShell? What command and account were used? Collection and command-line visibility depend on configuration Task Scheduler logs / audit When was the task registered, changed, and executed? Relevant logging may not have been enabled or retained PowerShell operational logs Is script-block or module content available? Logging policy and version affect visibility DNS Which name was queried, by which host, and at what time? A query alone does not prove a successful connection Network / proxy / firewall Was a connection established? What process or host initiated it? Network records may not identify the originating process Identity logs Was the account's sign-in or privilege use expected? Correlation requires correct time and identity context File telemetry Were scripts or payloads created, modified, or executed? Absence of a file event is not proof that no file existed

Build the timeline using UTC and preserve the original timestamps. Distinguish event time from collection or ingestion time.

docs.title: H1: Approved administration
docs.text:
Supporting evidence could include a known task owner, approved change, expected script path and signature, documented execution window, and matching activity on similarly managed endpoints.

Evidence against it could include an unknown registering account, unapproved arguments, an unexpected script location, or activity outside the change window.

docs.title: H2: Unauthorised but non-malicious activity
docs.text: A legitimate user may have created a task outside the change process. This can still be a policy or control issue even when there is no evidence of malware.

docs.title: H3: Malicious persistence or execution
docs.text:
Supporting evidence could include an unexplained task, concealed or user-writable execution path, obfuscated arguments, untrusted script content, suspicious account use, corroborated command-and-control activity, or related actions on other hosts.

No single indicator is sufficient. Corroborate the task, process, identity, and network evidence.

docs.title: Step 6 — Document the conclusion
docs.text:
Use a conclusion format that separates facts from interpretation:

  • Observed: what the source records directly show.
  • Correlated: which independent records align by host, identity, process identifier, and time.
  • Interpretation: what the combined evidence suggests.
  • Alternative explanations: plausible benign or non-malicious causes considered.
  • Confidence: low, moderate, or high, with a reason.
  • Gaps: missing logs, incomplete retention, uncertain attribution, or unverified ownership.
  • Next steps: further collection, owner confirmation, remediation, or escalation under approved procedures.

Example conclusion for this training case:

The available records establish that PowerShell executed shortly after a scheduled task was registered. They do not yet establish who authorised the task or whether the outbound connection was caused by that process. The case remains unresolved pending task-definition review, account validation, and process-to-network correlation.

docs.title: Step 7 — Response considerations
docs.text:
If evidence supports compromise, follow the organisation's incident-response process. Preserve volatile and relevant endpoint evidence, identify scope, and obtain the required approval for containment actions. Do not isolate a host, disable an account, or remove a task solely because an encoded command or one suspicious event was observed.

If the activity is approved, document the owner and change reference. If it is unauthorised but not malicious, route it through the appropriate control-remediation process.

docs.title: Analyst checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Original alert and raw records preserved
  • [ ] Host, user, and time zone confirmed
  • [ ] Process and parent process reviewed
  • [ ] Scheduled task definition and owner verified
  • [ ] PowerShell logging availability checked
  • [ ] DNS and network records correlated
  • [ ] Alternative explanations considered
  • [ ] Scope and affected assets assessed
  • [ ] Confidence and evidence gaps documented
  • [ ] Response actions aligned with approved procedure

docs.title: Enterprise-style cybersecurity home lab
docs.text:
Dependency-ordered build programme — reference guides, not yet hardware-tested

This programme has two distinct host tracks: Windows x64 and Apple-silicon Mac ARM64. They share security objectives, but not identical firewall appliances, guest architectures or hypervisor networking.

Build rule: complete each stage and its acceptance gate before proceeding. A SIEM is not installed until firewall, endpoint and network telemetry sources exist, produce events, and have a verified forwarding path.

docs.title: Correct dependency order
docs.text:
Stage Build activity Required outcome 0 Hardware and compatibility Host architecture, RAM, storage, guest and product support recorded 1 Windows host or Mac host Hypervisor installed; test VM boots and snapshot restore works 2 Network design Segments, addressing, adapter mapping and isolation boundaries documented 3 Windows OPNsense firewall or Mac ARM router Routing, default-deny policy, DNS/DHCP/NTP and egress controls validated 4 Operating systems and identity Domain controller, endpoints, Linux hosts, Kali and target deployed 5 Endpoint telemetry Windows Security/Sysmon and Linux/macOS source events verified locally 6 Network monitoring Firewall IDS, Suricata and Zeek visibility proven; logs written locally 7 Telemetry collection and forwarding Firewall syslog, endpoint events and sensor logs reach relay/collector 8 Elastic, Splunk or Wazuh One SIEM installed; each source ingested and searched successfully 9 Security Onion — optional x86-64 alternative Dedicated NSM/SOC deployment after network visibility is ready 10 Penetration testing Scope, isolation, target and telemetry gates passed 11 SOC validation End-to-end detection, investigation, evidence and cleanup demonstrated

Do not skip ahead to a SIEM because its installer is available. A running service or online agent does not prove that the required events are being collected.

docs.title: Windows x64 PC
docs.text:
This is the full x86-64 track. Choose one primary hypervisor: Hyper-V, VMware Workstation or VirtualBox. Run OPNsense as an x86-64 firewall VM with WAN plus separate internal network adapters. Start Suricata in alert-only IDS mode on relevant internal interfaces. Add a Zeek sensor only after a real packet mirror/tap or offline PCAP path is verified.

This track supports Windows Server/Windows 11 x64, Ubuntu x86-64, Kali x86-64, Splunk Enterprise on a supported x64 OS, and Security Onion x86-64 when hardware meets vendor requirements.

docs.title: Apple-silicon Mac
docs.text: Use VMware Fusion or another hypervisor supporting ARM64 guests. Use ARM64 Ubuntu, Kali and Windows 11 ARM images. OPNsense is x86-64 only; do not attempt to install it as an ARM64 guest. For a Mac-only isolated lab use the ARM64 Linux router/firewall path. It uses Ubuntu Server ARM64 and nftables; it is not an OPNsense replacement. Splunk Enterprise and Security Onion are not native ARM64 guest targets.

docs.title: Combining Windows and Mac
docs.text: Fusion host-only networks and Windows hypervisor private networks are local to their host; they do not automatically form one shared enterprise network. Start with two independently isolated labs. A single cross-host VLAN design requires a separate physical firewall/switch architecture. Never bridge REDTEAM or DMZ onto home Wi-Fi.

docs.title: Data-flow model
docs.text:
Endpoint events ───────────────> endpoint agent / forwarder ─┐
Firewall rule logs ────────────> syslog relay ───────────────┤
Firewall Suricata EVE alerts ──> syslog relay ───────────────┤
Zeek / sensor Suricata files ──> sensor collector/agent ─────┤
                                                            v
                                                 One selected SIEM
                                                            |
                                                  searches/detections
                                                            |
                                                  SOC investigation

Every arrow must be configured and tested. A firewall does not automatically export logs, and a sensor does not automatically send data to a SIEM.

docs.title: Resource planning
docs.text:
These are home-lab starting allocations, not universal vendor minimums:

Component Starting allocation Windows Server AD DS/DNS 2–4 vCPU, 6–8 GB RAM, 80 GB disk Windows 11 endpoint 2–4 vCPU, 6–8 GB RAM, 80 GB disk Ubuntu endpoint 2 vCPU, 2–4 GB RAM, 40–60 GB disk Kali 2–4 vCPU, 4–8 GB RAM, 60 GB disk Linux syslog relay 2 vCPU, 2–4 GB RAM, 30–50 GB disk Zeek/Suricata sensor 4 vCPU, 8 GB RAM, SSD-backed log storage Elastic single-node learning stack 4–8 vCPU, 12–16 GB RAM, 150–200 GB disk Splunk Enterprise learning stack 4 vCPU, 8–12 GB RAM, 100–150 GB disk; check current release requirements Wazuh all-in-one Use current official sizing; current quickstart reference is 4 vCPU, 8 GiB RAM, 50 GB for 90 days of indexed alert data Security Onion Standalone Vendor bare minimum: 4 CPU cores, 24 GB RAM, 200 GB storage, 2 NICs

Run one major SIEM stack at a time. Security Onion is a separate, resource-intensive platform.

docs.title: Evidence standard
docs.text:
For every stage record host/guest architecture, versions, checksums, VM resources, adapter mapping, IPs/routes, firewall rules, source event, collector receipt, SIEM document, timestamps, expected/actual results, rollback and cleanup. Never publish employer logs, customer data, credentials, tokens or private certificates.

Status: These are build instructions. Do not label a stage “lab-tested” until executed on the target hardware with sanitised evidence.

docs.title: Master build sequence — dependency gates
docs.text:
Canonical execution order — reference guide, not yet hardware-tested

This is the authoritative Phase 6 order. Follow it from an empty host. Product pages contain installation details; this page defines prerequisites and pass/fail gates. If a gate fails, stop and fix it.

docs.title: Stage 0 — select platform and verify support
docs.text:
1. Complete Hardware & Compatibility.
  2. Record CPU architecture, host OS/build, RAM, free SSD space and hypervisor version.
  3. Choose one primary Windows hypervisor.
  4. On Apple Silicon, use ARM64 guest images only.
  5. Decide whether Windows and Mac remain separate lab islands or will later be joined using a physical firewall/VLAN design.

Gate 0: every guest and product has a supported architecture. OPNsense and Security Onion are x86-64. Splunk Enterprise requires a supported x64 platform. Apple Silicon cannot run these x86-64 guests natively.

docs.title: Stage 1 — host and hypervisor
docs.text:
Follow Windows Host Setup, Mac Host Setup, and VirtualBox Host Setup if selected.

  1. Install one hypervisor from its official source.
  2. Create VM, ISO, export, evidence and backup folders on SSD.
  3. Download official guest images and verify checksums/signatures.
  4. Create one small Ubuntu test VM of the correct architecture.
  5. Verify boot, networking and time.
  6. Snapshot, restore and boot again.

Gate 1: host reboot does not break the hypervisor; test guest boots/restores; no guest is bridged to the physical LAN without an explicit design.

docs.title: Stage 2 — design and create networks
docs.text:
Follow Network Design. Check example subnets against home LAN, VPN and existing routes.

Segment Example subnet Purpose MGMT 10.10.10.0/24 Admin workstation and management UIs ENDPOINT 10.10.20.0/24 Windows/Linux/Mac test endpoints SERVER 10.10.30.0/24 AD DS/DNS, syslog relay and selected SIEM REDTEAM 10.10.40.0/24 Kali assessment source SENSOR 10.10.50.0/24 Sensor management/capture design DMZ 10.10.60.0/24 Vulnerable targets

Gate 2: segments exist; VM NICs are mapped; no DHCP overlap, subnet overlap or unintended bridged adapter.

docs.title: Windows x64
docs.text: Follow OPNsense Firewall & Routing. Create an x86-64 OPNsense VM with WAN on hypervisor NAT and internal adapters for MGMT, ENDPOINT, SERVER, REDTEAM and DMZ. Map interfaces by MAC, not assumed adapter order. Configure DNS/DHCP only where required, default-deny between segments, narrowly scoped AD/management/telemetry rules, temporary update egress and encrypted configuration backup.

docs.title: Apple Silicon Mac
docs.text:
Follow Mac ARM Router & Firewall. Use Ubuntu Server ARM64 with nftables and separate Fusion private networks. This is not OPNsense. If Fusion cannot create enough isolated networks, stop; do not collapse all guests onto one host-only network and call it segmented.

Gate 3: verify DHCP/static addressing, DNS, gateway, allowed and denied TCP flows, firewall logs and routes. Kali/DMZ must not reach home LAN or MGMT.

docs.title: Stage 4 — operating systems and identity
docs.text:
Follow Operating Systems & Identity.

Windows x64 track: Windows Server on SERVER; create a private lab-only AD domain such as lab.psv.test; Windows 11 x64 on ENDPOINT; Ubuntu; Kali on REDTEAM; vulnerable target on DMZ.

Mac ARM64 track: Ubuntu Server ARM64, Kali ARM64 and architecture-compatible target VM/container. Windows 11 ARM is optional only after verifying the exact agent/driver support. Do not assume x64 agents work on Windows ARM.

Gate 4: record hostnames, OS versions, architecture, IPs, routes, DNS, time and NICs. Domain join works where used. Kali reaches only its scoped target. DMZ has no unrestricted Internet/home-LAN path.

docs.title: Stage 5 — generate endpoint telemetry locally
docs.text:
Follow Windows Endpoint Telemetry.

  1. Configure Windows Advanced Audit Policy through a lab-only GPO.
  2. Install/configure Sysmon using Microsoft's current instructions and a reviewed configuration.
  3. Generate a benign process-creation event and verify it in the local Sysmon Operational channel.
  4. Generate a controlled Windows Security event and verify it locally.
  5. On Linux, enable required auditd/journald sources and verify local records.
  6. On macOS, use only telemetry sources supported by the chosen agent and OS version.

Gate 5: raw source event exists locally with host, timestamp and event identity. Do not troubleshoot SIEM ingestion before this passes.

docs.title: Stage 6 — firewall and network monitoring
docs.text:
Follow Network Monitoring.

  1. On Windows OPNsense, enable Suricata in alert-only IDS mode on relevant internal interfaces, not only WAN. WAN capture after NAT may lose original internal source identity.
  2. Enable logging on the firewall rules used for pass/block tests.
  3. Generate known allowed and denied connections; verify firewall logs show rule and endpoints.
  4. Enable OPNsense Suricata EVE/syslog output and verify the local alert.
  5. Install Zeek only after a real packet mirror/tap is configured. Hyper-V port mirroring works only when source and destination adapters share the relevant virtual switch; Workstation/Fusion/VirtualBox promiscuous mode is not a universal SPAN.
  6. Generate known DNS/HTTP traffic and verify Zeek logs and Suricata EVE JSON locally.
  7. Record exactly which segments/interfaces are visible.

On Mac ARM, use supported ARM64 Zeek/Suricata builds only after verifying packet visibility. Verify nftables firewall logs locally.

Gate 6: firewall pass/block events, IDS alerts, Zeek logs (if enabled) and endpoint events exist locally. Packet visibility is proven with a known flow.

docs.title: Stage 7 — telemetry collection and forwarding
docs.text:
Follow Telemetry Collection & Forwarding.

  1. Create a Linux syslog relay on SERVER.
  2. Configure OPNsense or the Mac Linux router to send firewall events to the relay.
  3. Verify messages arrive and are written to the expected per-source files.
  4. Verify Zeek/Suricata files exist, are readable and rotate safely.
  5. Prepare the chosen SIEM's agent/forwarder path on relay and sensor.
  6. Keep endpoint collection explicit: Windows Event Channels/Sysmon, Linux journald/auditd and macOS Unified Logging where supported.
  7. Verify source → relay/file → collector with identity and timestamp intact.

Gate 7: each required source reaches the relay/collector before SIEM installation. Only required source IPs and ports are allowed.

docs.title: Stage 8 — install one SIEM and connect sources
docs.text:
Choose one stack per iteration:

  • Elastic: Fleet/Elastic Agent, Windows and System integrations, Filestream for firewall/sensor files.
  • Splunk: Enterprise on supported x64; Universal Forwarder monitors endpoint, relay and sensor files. Use rsyslog/syslog-ng plus UF or Splunk Connect for Syslog, not direct Splunk UDP input as default.
  • Wazuh: central stack plus agents on endpoints, relay and sensor; Logcollector monitors firewall/sensor files. Use relay-file-plus-agent rather than relying on direct manager syslog listener across versions.

For each stack, confirm current OS/architecture support and licence; configure TLS/authentication; connect one source at a time; inspect raw events and parsed fields; measure ingestion delay; check duplicates; then add detections.

Gate 8: every required source has a raw searchable event with correct source/host/time fields and measured ingest delay. Agent online alone does not pass.

docs.title: Stage 9 — optional Security Onion
docs.text: Security Onion is x86-64 only and resource intensive. Build on Windows x64 or dedicated x86-64 hardware after network and packet visibility stages. It is an alternative integrated NSM/SOC platform, not an ARM Mac guest or a prerequisite for other SIEMs.

docs.title: Stage 10 — controlled penetration testing
docs.text:
Follow Penetration Testing. Define target IPs/ports and test window; re-check Kali REDTEAM isolation and DMZ egress; record baseline firewall/endpoint/sensor events; run only the lab-owned test; correlate firewall, IDS, Zeek, endpoint and SIEM records; remove temporary rules and restore the target.

Gate 10: scope and isolation pass before scanning. Unexpected reachability is a stop condition.

docs.title: Stage 11 — SOC validation
docs.text: Follow SOC Validation Exercises. Test benign process creation, account/group change, DNS/HTTP and blocked network activity. Preserve source event, relay record, SIEM document, query, rule/version, alert, timeline, analyst conclusion and cleanup.

docs.title: Stage 12 — operations and recovery
docs.text: Back up firewall configuration, AD/system state, SIEM configuration and required data separately from snapshots. Document retention, patch windows, credential rotation, agent health, storage growth and restore tests. Re-test segmentation after hypervisor/firewall/NIC changes.

docs.title: Stop conditions
docs.text: Stop if a guest has an unexpected bridged NIC, Kali/DMZ can reach home LAN, interface mapping is uncertain, source events are absent, sensor feed is unproven, collector files are empty, or product architecture is unsupported. Fix the dependency; do not bypass it by disabling security controls.

docs.title: Lab 5 — Elastic SIEM, Fleet and endpoint telemetry
docs.text: Build guide — not yet lab-tested

docs.title: Mandatory prerequisites — complete before installing Elastic
docs.text:
Do not start this SIEM until Stages 0–7 in Master Build Sequence pass. OPNsense firewall/Suricata events must already reach the Linux syslog relay; Zeek/Suricata files must exist on the sensor; Windows Security/Sysmon and Linux events must exist locally. Follow Telemetry Collection & Forwarding.

For firewall and sensor logs, install Elastic Agent on the relay/sensor and use the supported Custom Logs (Filestream) integration for written log files. Use the Windows and System integrations for endpoints. A Fleet Server being online does not prove that syslog or JSON files are ingested. Verify each raw event and data stream separately.

docs.title: 1. Topology and sizing
docs.text: Use a fresh supported Ubuntu Server VM on the Windows x64 PC: 4–8 vCPU, 12–16 GB RAM and 150–200 GB SSD-backed virtual disk as a home-lab starting point. Run Elastic alone initially. This is a single-node learning deployment, not production HA. Keep Elasticsearch and Kibana on the same version. Check the current Elastic support matrix for the selected OS and architecture.

docs.title: 2. Install Elasticsearch 9.x from the official APT repository
docs.text:
The following follows Elastic's currently documented 9.x Debian package instructions. If a new major release is available when you build, use that major version's official instructions and change the repository path consistently.

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y wget gnupg apt-transport-https
sudo install -d -m 0755 /usr/share/keyrings
wget -qO - https://artifacts.elastic.co/GPG-KEY-elasticsearch | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /usr/share/keyrings/elasticsearch-keyring.gpg
echo "deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/elasticsearch-keyring.gpg] https://artifacts.elastic.co/packages/9.x/apt stable main" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/elastic-9.x.list
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y elasticsearch

Start and enable Elasticsearch:

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable elasticsearch.service
sudo systemctl start elasticsearch.service
sudo systemctl status elasticsearch --no-pager
sudo /usr/share/elasticsearch/bin/elasticsearch-reset-password -u elastic

Save the generated password securely. First startup enables security and creates TLS certificates. Do not disable authentication or TLS.

Verify local HTTPS (enter the password when prompted):

curl --cacert /etc/elasticsearch/certs/http_ca.crt -u elastic https://localhost:9200

A successful response includes cluster/node and version details. If the certificate path differs, inspect the package output and actual certificate location. Do not use an insecure TLS bypass as a permanent workaround.

docs.title: 3. Install Kibana from the same repository
docs.text:
Use the same Elastic 9.x APT repository and install the same release family:

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y kibana
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable kibana.service
sudo systemctl start kibana.service
sudo systemctl status kibana --no-pager

Generate a Kibana enrollment token on the Elasticsearch host:

sudo /usr/share/elasticsearch/bin/elasticsearch-create-enrollment-token -s kibana

Open the Kibana setup URL shown by the service status, enter the enrollment token, complete the verification-code step, then sign in with the elastic account. Enrollment tokens expire; generate a new token if required. Follow the current Kibana Debian installation guide if the setup wizard differs.

Restrict Kibana access to MGMT. Do not expose port 5601 to the public Internet.

docs.title: 4. Configure Fleet
docs.text:
1. Open Kibana from the management workstation.
  2. Navigate to Management → Fleet.
  3. Follow the Fleet Server setup wizard for the deployment type.
  4. Use a stable lab DNS name/IP reachable from endpoint VMs.
  5. Create the Fleet Server policy and enrollment token.
  6. Use the exact install/enrollment command generated by the wizard on each endpoint.
  7. Keep TLS trust configured. Treat enrollment tokens as secrets; never publish them.

For a small lab, Fleet Server may share the Ubuntu VM, but check current Fleet sizing and support requirements. If the wizard or load requires a separate Fleet Server, create another VM.

docs.title: 5. Windows Sysmon integration
docs.text:
1. On PSV-W11-01, install Sysmon using Microsoft's official instructions.
  2. Confirm Event Viewer → Applications and Services Logs → Microsoft → Windows → Sysmon → Operational receives Event ID 1.
  3. In Kibana → Integrations, add the Windows integration to the Windows endpoint policy.
  4. Enable Sysmon Operational channel collection.
  5. Wait for the policy to apply, then launch Notepad on the endpoint.
  6. Inspect the raw event in Discover and record the actual data stream and field names.

Do not assume dataset/field mappings are identical across integration releases. Inspect the raw document.

docs.title: 6. Linux endpoint integration
docs.text:
1. Add the System integration to a Linux endpoint policy.
  2. Enrol the Ubuntu endpoint using the Fleet-generated command.
  3. Confirm system metrics arrive.
  4. Add Auditd integration only after auditd is installed and configured on the endpoint.
  5. Confirm the audit source and event fields separately from system metrics.

docs.title: 7. Search and test
docs.text:
After confirming the real data stream and ECS mappings, a starting KQL search for Sysmon process creation is:

event.code : "1" and process.name : "notepad.exe"

Create a test detection only after verifying the fields. The Phase 5 PowerShell analytic assumes ECS process fields; adapt it to the raw event and dataset actually ingested. Run positive and negative tests and record the raw event, alert, timestamps, agent version and ingest delay.

docs.title: 8. Troubleshooting
docs.text:
sudo journalctl -u elasticsearch -n 100 --no-pager
sudo journalctl -u kibana -n 100 --no-pager

For offline agents, check Fleet URL resolution, TLS trust, firewall, policy and the agent status command. For no Sysmon data, first prove the local event exists; then check agent integration, channel subscription, ingest errors and data stream. For high memory pressure, reduce active VMs; do not arbitrarily change JVM heap.

docs.title: 9. Cleanup
docs.text: Unenrol agents through Fleet, stop services cleanly and retain only sanitised evidence. Follow Elastic's package removal/data-directory procedures if deleting the lab. Never commit passwords, tokens, certificates or production telemetry.

docs.title: Lab — Firewall, routing, IDS and firewall-log generation
docs.text:
Mandatory before telemetry forwarding — reference guide, not yet hardware-tested

This page is the Windows x64 OPNsense implementation. For an Apple-silicon Mac-only build use Mac ARM Router & Firewall. OPNsense supports x86-64, not ARM64.

docs.title: 1. Windows OPNsense topology
docs.text:
Create one x86-64 OPNsense VM with six adapters:

Role Network Address WAN Hypervisor NAT only DHCP from hypervisor NAT MGMT Internal/host-only 10.10.10.1/24 ENDPOINT Private/host-only 10.10.20.1/24 SERVER Private/host-only 10.10.30.1/24 REDTEAM Private/host-only 10.10.40.1/24 DMZ Private/host-only 10.10.60.1/24

The SENSOR capture path is separate. Do not assume a routed SENSOR interface receives copies of all packets. Use OPNsense IDS on relevant routed interfaces or a separately verified mirror/tap for Zeek.

docs.title: 2. Create the firewall VM
docs.text:
On Windows x64 use the selected hypervisor. Starting allocation: 2–4 vCPU, 4 GB RAM and 20 GB disk. OPNsense recommends at least 4 GB RAM and an 8 GB virtual disk for virtual installation; allocate more for IDS/log retention.

  • Hyper-V: create Generation 2 VM; follow current OPNsense Hyper-V notes for Secure Boot. Add six NICs and attach each to its intended switch.
  • VMware Workstation: add six NICs; WAN on NAT, internal roles on separate host-only networks.
  • VirtualBox: follow VirtualBox Host Setup; WAN on NAT, MGMT host-only, remaining segments named Internal Networks.

Record every virtual NIC MAC before boot. At OPNsense console map roles by MAC and link state. Adapter number is not a reliable interface identifier.

docs.title: 3. Install OPNsense
docs.text:
1. Download the current x86-64 DVD ISO from the official OPNsense site and verify its checksum.
  2. Boot and follow the current official installer. Installation erases the selected virtual disk.
  3. Set a strong unique administrative password.
  4. Reboot and detach the ISO.
  5. Assign WAN and internal interfaces using the MAC mapping.
  6. Configure WAN by DHCP from hypervisor NAT and internal addresses from the topology table.
  7. From MGMT, open the OPNsense HTTPS UI. Do not expose GUI/SSH on WAN.

docs.title: 4. DNS, DHCP and time
docs.text:
1. Configure Unbound DNS to listen only on required internal interfaces.
  2. Create DHCP scopes only for client networks; keep DC, relay and SIEM static/reserved.
  3. Do not run a second DHCP service on the same segment.
  4. Use a consistent time source/timezone for all guests.
  5. For AD DS, domain clients use the domain controller for DNS; configure upstream resolution deliberately.

docs.title: 5. Least-privilege policy
docs.text:
Retain a safe management path and console access before narrowing rules.

  • MGMT: allow only named admin workstation to firewall and server management ports.
  • ENDPOINT: allow DNS/NTP, required AD DS traffic to DC, and later telemetry to relay/SIEM on explicit ports.
  • SERVER: allow management from MGMT, required endpoint-to-server services and relay-to-SIEM forwarding.
  • REDTEAM: allow Kali only to the written target IP/ports in DMZ; deny home LAN, MGMT and unrelated destinations.
  • DMZ: allow only target service ports; deny initiation to MGMT, SERVER, ENDPOINT and home LAN.
  • WAN: no inbound management. Update egress is temporary and controlled.

Do not guess Active Directory ports. Use Microsoft's current port documentation and test the exact services enabled, including dynamic RPC.

docs.title: 6. Generate firewall logs
docs.text:
OPNsense does not necessarily log every pass rule by default. Edit the specific firewall rules used for allow/deny exercises and enable the rule's Log option.

  1. Generate a known allowed connection, such as endpoint DNS to the lab resolver.
  2. Generate a known denied connection, such as REDTEAM to a prohibited MGMT address.
  3. Open the live firewall log and verify source, destination, port, interface, rule/action and timestamp.
  4. Save sanitised evidence.

If a rule is not logged, inspect its Log setting and live-log filters before concluding enforcement failed.

docs.title: 7. Enable Suricata IDS in alert-only mode
docs.text:
OPNsense Intrusion Detection is based on Suricata. Start with IDS/alert-only; do not begin with inline IPS blocking.

  1. Open Services → Intrusion Detection.
  2. Enable the service and select the internal interfaces carrying traffic of interest. WAN-only capture may show NAT-translated addresses.
  3. Set HOME_NET to the lab subnets actually protected.
  4. Enable a reviewed ruleset such as ET Open and understand its licence/update process.
  5. Update rules and check service health.
  6. Generate controlled test traffic and verify the service processes packets and produces the expected alert when the selected rule matches.
  7. Confirm the alert in the OPNsense IDS view and local log.

OPNsense offers different capture modes and driver requirements. IDS is the safer initial mode. IPS/netmap can interrupt traffic and may require disabling hardware offloads; do not enable IPS until exact release, NIC driver and recovery access are validated.

docs.title: 8. Enable EVE/syslog for later forwarding
docs.text:
1. Enable EVE syslog output in Intrusion Detection if available in the installed release.
  2. In System → Settings → Logging → Remote, add the Linux relay destination.
  3. Select Suricata/application filters where the UI provides them and choose the transport/port configured on the relay.
  4. Apply changes.
  5. Generate a known IDS event and confirm it reaches the relay.

Follow Telemetry Collection & Forwarding for the complete relay and SIEM collector setup. Do not install a SIEM before the source-to-relay test passes.

docs.title: 9. Validation and backup
docs.text:
• [ ] NIC roles mapped by MAC.
  • [ ] Internal addresses, DHCP and DNS correct.
  • [ ] Broad allow rules narrowed.
  • [ ] Allowed and denied flows visible in firewall logs.
  • [ ] REDTEAM/DMZ cannot reach home LAN or MGMT.
  • [ ] Suricata IDS sees intended internal traffic.
  • [ ] EVE/syslog test event reaches relay.
  • [ ] Encrypted configuration backup exported outside the VM.

If isolation fails, disconnect Kali and DMZ guests and correct the network/firewall mapping before continuing.

docs.title: Mac ARM64 lab — Linux router and firewall
docs.text:
Mac-only alternative — not OPNsense, not yet hardware-tested

Apple-silicon Macs cannot run OPNsense as an ARM64 guest because OPNsense supports x86-64. This guide uses Ubuntu Server ARM64 with nftables for a segmented Mac-only lab. It is not a feature-equivalent OPNsense replacement. If OPNsense is mandatory, use a separate x86-64 physical appliance or the Windows x64 OPNsense VM.

docs.title: 1. Preconditions
docs.text:
• Apple-silicon Mac and VMware Fusion.
  • Fusion release that exposes enough independent custom/private host networks.
  • Ubuntu Server ARM64 ISO from Ubuntu.
  • No REDTEAM or DMZ guest connected to Bridged networking.

If the installed Fusion release cannot create independent networks for the segments below, stop. Do not pretend one host-only network provides segmentation.

docs.title: 2. Create Fusion networks
docs.text:
Open Fusion network preferences and inspect available networks. Keep the default NAT network for router WAN only. Create independent private/host-only networks for MGMT, ENDPOINT, SERVER, REDTEAM and DMZ. Disable Fusion DHCP on internal networks if the Linux router will provide DHCP; otherwise use static addressing consistently and do not enable a second DHCP server.

Network Subnet Router address MGMT 10.10.10.0/24 10.10.10.1 ENDPOINT 10.10.20.0/24 10.10.20.1 SERVER 10.10.30.0/24 10.10.30.1 REDTEAM 10.10.40.0/24 10.10.40.1 DMZ 10.10.60.0/24 10.10.60.1

Record the actual Fusion network names and verify subnets before configuring guests. If Fusion assigns different ranges, change the plan consistently.

docs.title: 3. Create the Ubuntu ARM64 router VM
docs.text:
1. Download Ubuntu Server ARM64 and verify its published checksum.
  2. Create PSV-MAC-RTR01 with 2–4 vCPU, 4 GB RAM and 30 GB disk.
  3. Add six adapters: NAT for WAN and one for each internal segment.
  4. Install Ubuntu Server and create a named sudo user.

  5. Update, reboot and identify interfaces/MAC addresses:

    uname -m ip -br link ip -br address ip route

Expected architecture is aarch64. Record every NIC MAC and map it to its Fusion network before configuration. Do not guess interface names.

docs.title: 4. Configure interface addressing
docs.text:
Use Netplan MAC matching so Linux interface enumeration changes do not silently swap network roles. Configure: - WAN: DHCP from Fusion NAT; this is the only interface with a default route. - MGMT: 10.10.10.1/24. - ENDPOINT: 10.10.20.1/24. - SERVER: 10.10.30.1/24. - REDTEAM: 10.10.40.1/24. - DMZ: 10.10.60.1/24.

Use the actual MAC values in Netplan. Do not set default gateways on internal interfaces. Validate Netplan before applying; keep the Fusion console open in case remote access is lost.

docs.title: 5. Enable routing and firewall
docs.text:
Install the Ubuntu-supported nftables package. Enable IPv4 forwarding using a persistent sysctl setting and verify it is active. Keep IPv6 forwarding disabled unless you have designed and tested an equivalent IPv6 policy; an IPv4-only ruleset must not leave an IPv6 bypass.

Create a persistent nftables ruleset with: - Default-drop input and forward chains. - Loopback and established/related traffic allowed. - Management access only from the named MGMT admin host. - Explicit DNS/NTP, AD DS and telemetry flows added only when required. - REDTEAM-to-DMZ limited to the written target IP/ports. - DMZ-to-MGMT/SERVER/ENDPOINT/home LAN denied. - Source NAT only for the selected internal subnets allowed temporary update egress.

Build and validate rules from the Fusion console. Use nftables syntax-check mode before applying a file. Keep a known-good snapshot and do not paste an unreviewed generic firewall script into a live host.

docs.title: 6. DHCP and DNS
docs.text: Start with static addresses to prove routing and firewall policy. Once stable, add one DHCP service (for example, dnsmasq) on the router and one non-overlapping scope per client segment. Disable Fusion DHCP on those segments. For an AD domain, domain clients must use the domain controller for DNS; configure forwarding/resolution deliberately.

docs.title: 7. Validate isolation
docs.text:
From each guest:

ip -br address
ip route
ip neigh

Test: - Each guest reaches its own router interface. - Only explicitly allowed cross-segment services work. - Kali reaches only the scoped DMZ target. - DMZ cannot initiate to MGMT, SERVER, ENDPOINT or home LAN. - No guest has a second NAT or Bridged NIC bypassing the router.

Check nftables counters/logs for allowed and denied flows. Ping failure is not sufficient evidence.

docs.title: 8. Firewall logging
docs.text: Add nftables log statements to selected deny rules with a unique prefix. Verify the messages appear locally in journald. Configure rsyslog to write those messages to a dedicated file, then follow Telemetry Collection & Forwarding. Do not assume nftables automatically exports logs remotely.

docs.title: 9. Limitations
docs.text: This Linux router does not provide OPNsense's GUI, DHCP/DNS integration, Suricata plugin or configuration backup interface. Install ARM64 Zeek/Suricata separately only after verifying package support and packet visibility. Do not claim full network visibility without a proven mirror/tap or inline path.
